name: The Reaction Quotient and Equilibrium Constant
what: This subtopic covers how to write equilibrium expressions, calculate the equilibrium constant K and the reaction quotient Q, and use the relationship between Q and K to determine the direction in which a reaction will shift.
why: K and Q provide a quantitative way to describe where a reaction sits relative to equilibrium at any moment. These calculations are heavily assessed in VCE Chemistry and underpin the ability to predict reaction behaviour and solve multi-step equilibrium problems.

items.title: I can write the equilibrium constant expression for a given reaction
items.what: The equilibrium constant expression K is written as the product of the molar concentrations of the products, each raised to the power of their stoichiometric coefficient, divided by the same for the reactants.
items.why: Writing the correct expression is the starting point for all K calculations. Errors in the expression (wrong coefficients as powers, products and reactants swapped) will produce incorrect values for K and lose marks across all related questions.
items.example: For 2SO2(g) + O2(g) = 2SO3(g), the expression is K = [SO3]^2 / ([SO2]^2 x [O2]). Note that the coefficient 2 for SO2 and SO3 becomes the power in the expression.

items.title: I can determine the position of equilibrium based on the value of K
items.what: A large value of K (much greater than 1) indicates that products are favoured at equilibrium - the reaction has proceeded significantly toward the product side. A small K (much less than 1) indicates reactants are favoured.
items.why: K gives a direct, quantitative snapshot of where the equilibrium position lies. This allows chemists and students to immediately assess whether a reaction is useful for producing a desired product under given conditions.
items.example: The reaction H2(g) + I2(g) = 2HI(g) at 440 degrees C has K approximately equal to 49.5. This large value indicates that at equilibrium, HI is strongly favoured over H2 and I2, meaning the forward reaction has proceeded extensively.

items.title: I can use the equilibrium expression to calculate K or an unknown equilibrium concentration
items.what: Given equilibrium concentrations of all species, K can be calculated by direct substitution into the expression. If K and some equilibrium concentrations are known, an unknown concentration can be found by rearranging the expression. ICE tables can be used when only initial concentrations and partial equilibrium data are given.
items.why: This is a core calculation skill for VCE Chemistry. Questions may provide initial concentrations and one equilibrium value, requiring students to use stoichiometric ratios to determine the rest before calculating K.
items.example: For N2O4(g) = 2NO2(g), if 0.27 mol of N2O4 is placed in a 1.0 L flask and 0.14 mol remains at equilibrium, the change in N2O4 is 0.13 M, so [NO2] = 0.26 M. Then K = (0.26)^2 / 0.14 = 0.48 M.

items.title: I can calculate the reaction quotient Q, including units, for a given equilibrium system
items.what: Q is calculated using the same expression as K, but with concentrations taken at any point in time rather than at equilibrium. The units of Q and K depend on the stoichiometry of the specific reaction, and are found by applying index laws to the units of concentration (M).
items.why: Q allows students to assess a reaction's position at any moment in time. The ability to determine units is also directly assessed in VCE and requires careful application of index laws to avoid errors.

items.title: I can determine how the position of equilibrium will shift by comparing Q and K
items.what: If Q is less than K, the reaction must produce more products to reach equilibrium, so the forward reaction is favoured. If Q is greater than K, the reaction must produce more reactants, so the reverse reaction is favoured. If Q equals K, the system is already at equilibrium.
items.why: Comparing Q to K is a powerful and reliable method for predicting reaction direction. It works in situations where reasoning from Le Chatelier's principle alone is insufficient, and it is a common type of VCE examination question.
items.example: For Fe3+(aq) + SCN-(aq) = FeSCN2+(aq) with K = 7.89 x 10^2, if [Fe3+] = 0.002, [SCN-] = 0.015 and [FeSCN2+] = 0.01, then Q = 0.01 / (0.002 x 0.015) = 333. Since Q (333) is less than K (789), the forward reaction is favoured.
